title: Go, and Be a Blessing
sum: After eleven chapters of a widening curse, from Eden to Babel, God speaks to one man. Abram is told to leave land, clan and father's house for a land he has not seen, and is given a sevenfold promise: a great nation, blessing, a great name, and blessing for all the clans of the earth through him. At seventy-five he goes, with Sarai, Lot and their household, and walks the length of Canaan, building altars at Shechem and near Bethel.

Then the promise is put at risk almost at once. A famine drives Abram to Egypt, and to save himself he has Sarai call herself his sister. She is taken into Pharaoh's house. The LORD strikes Pharaoh with plagues, and the foreign king, not the man of faith, speaks the chapter's moral question: "What is this you have done to me?"
readings: Read as history

A real migration of a herding family from upper Mesopotamia into Canaan and down to Egypt in a time of famine, something Egyptian records show happened often (a well-known tomb painting at Beni Hasan, about 1890 BC, shows a group of Asiatic traders entering Egypt). The tradition dates Abram to about 2000 BC or a little later.
Read as theology

The turning point of the Bible's story. Genesis 1–11 shows sin spreading to the whole world; 12:1–3 begins God's answer through one family "for all the clans of the earth." The rest of Scripture can be read as the story of how that promise is kept.
Read as character study
Abram obeys without a word in 12:4 and fails in 12:13. Genesis does not hide its heroes' weakness: faith and fear sit in the same man in the same chapter.

views.L: Abram was a historical man of about 2100–1900 BC (or, on other counts, about 1800 BC) whom God called from Ur and Haran. The chapter records his real journey and a real lapse; the plagues are God's actual protection of the promised mother.
views.F: The chapter is built as a counterpoint to Babel: there people tried to "make a name" for themselves (11:4); here God promises to make Abram's name great. The point is theological: blessing comes by God's call, not human building.
views.C: Most critical scholars assign 12:1–4a and 12:6–20 to the Yahwist (J), with 12:4b–5 from the Priestly writer (P), who supplies ages and lists. Few think the stories can be dated to the second millennium BC; John Van Seters and Thomas Thompson argued in the 1970s that their customs fit the first millennium better. Many see 12:1–3 as written to give exiles or a struggling kingdom a founding promise.
views.J: This chapter begins the weekly Torah reading Lekh Lekha. The rabbis count the call as the first of Abraham's ten trials (Avot 5:3) and see in the Egypt story the template for Israel's own descent, slavery and exodus. Ramban faulted Abraham here; Rashi defends him.

deep.b:
God's words in 12:2–3 are often counted as seven promises: (1) a great nation, (2) blessing, (3) a great name, (4) "be a blessing," (5) blessing for those who bless, (6) a curse for the one who despises, and (7) blessing for all the clans of the earth. The land is added in 12:7. These become the backbone of Genesis: each later scene puts one of them at risk (no son, a wife taken, a land held by others) and shows God keeping it.

The same promises return to Isaac (26:3–4) and Jacob (28:13–14), and the New Testament opens by calling Jesus "the son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1). Paul makes 12:3 the heart of his case that Gentiles are included in God's people by faith (Galatians 3:8).

The Beni Hasan tomb painting, from the tomb of the official Khnumhotep II in Middle Egypt (about 1890 BC), shows thirty-seven "Asiatics" from Canaan or Syria, in bright woven clothes, arriving with donkeys to trade. It is often reproduced in Bible atlases to show what travelers like Abram may have looked like. It does not mention Abram or any biblical person.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the famine as the first test of the promise
deep.body: My own reading, close to what Wenham and others say: the chapter sets up a pattern that runs through Abraham's life. Every promise in 12:2–3 is followed by a threat to it: the land (famine, 12:10), the wife who must bear the heir (12:15), and later the heir himself (22:2). Each time the threat comes from inside the land of promise or from Abram's own fear. The point seems to be that the promise survives not because Abram guards it well, but because God does.

echoes: Joshua 24:2–3; Acts 7:2–5; Hebrews 11:8–10; Galatians 3:6–9; Galatians 3:16; Romans 4:13; Isaiah 51:2; Exodus 12:35–36; Psalm 105:12–15

settings.to: Abram son of Terah, living in Haran in upper Mesopotamia
settings.when: While Abram is in Haran, where his father had stopped on the way to Canaan (11:31)
settings.why: To call Abram to leave his land, his kin and his father's house for a land not yet shown. God promises him a great nation, blessing and a great name, so that all the clans of the earth will find blessing in him. It is God's answer to Genesis 1–11: the builders of Babel tried to make a name, and God gives one.
settings.readers: For Israel this was the charter of their people and their land. For exiles in Babylon it was a call to leave Mesopotamia again, as their father had. Paul reads the promise as the gospel announced ahead of time to the nations (Galatians 3:8).
views: Most translations and Paul read 12:3 as the clans of the earth receiving blessing through Abram.
Some Jewish and critical readers take the verb to mean that the nations will use Abram's name when they bless each other, as in "May you be like Abraham."

settings.to: His wife Sarai
settings.when: As they come near Egypt to escape a famine
settings.why: To have Sarai say she is his sister, so that he will survive and be treated well. At the first test, the man of the promise puts the promised mother at risk. The foreign king, struck by plagues, is the one who rebukes him (12:18–19).
settings.readers: For Israel this was its own later story played out ahead of time. There is famine, a going down to Egypt, plagues on Pharaoh, and leaving with great wealth.
views: E. A. Speiser explained the wife-sister stories by contracts from Nuzi in which a wife was also adopted as a sister, a higher status.
Samuel Greengus showed that the Nuzi texts give no ground for a "sister-wife," and most scholars now read the stories as plain deception for safety.

title: Lot Chooses by Sight
sum: Abram comes back from Egypt rich and returns to his first altar near Bethel. But his flocks and Lot's are too many for the same pastures, and their herders quarrel. Abram, the elder, gives Lot the first choice of land. Lot looks east, sees the Jordan Plain watered like Eden, and moves his tents as far as Sodom, whose people were "great sinners against the LORD."

Once Lot is gone, God tells Abram to look north, south, east and west: all of it will belong to him and his offspring, who will be as many as the dust of the earth. Abram settles by the great trees of Mamre at Hebron and builds another altar.
readings: Read as history
A believable picture of two herding clans competing for water and grass among settled Canaanite towns, the kind of tension seen in many ancient and modern pastoral societies.
Read as a moral story

The chapter contrasts two kinds of choosing. Lot "raised his eyes" and chose by what looked best (13:10). Abram let go, and then God told him to "raise your eyes" and gave him everything he could see (13:14). Christian tradition has long preached it this way (Hebrews 11:9–10).

views.L: A true episode from Abram's life. The Jordan Plain was then lush, before the destruction of Sodom changed the region (19:24–28).
views.F: The chapter's key is sight: Lot sees and chooses, God tells Abram to see and receive. It also quietly removes Lot as Abram's possible heir, sharpening the question of who will inherit the promise.
views.C: Mostly assigned to J, with P supplying 13:6 and 13:11b–12a. Critical scholars often read the story as explaining Israel's relation to its eastern neighbors, Moab and Ammon, who were traced to Lot (19:36–38): kin, but outside the land.
views.J: The rabbis were hard on Lot: Genesis Rabbah says his choosing of Sodom showed he was drawn to its immorality, and Rashi says that when Lot "set out eastward" (miqqedem) he was moving away from the One who was "before" (qadmon) the world. Abram's generosity is held up as a model of pursuing peace.

echoes: Psalm 133:1; Hebrews 11:9–10; 2 Peter 2:7–8; Joshua 1:3; Romans 4:13; Ezekiel 16:49–50

settings.to: Lot, his nephew, whose herders are quarreling with his own
settings.when: Back near Bethel after Egypt, when the land cannot carry both their flocks
settings.why: To end the quarrel between kinsmen by giving the younger man first choice of land, "for we are brothers." Abram trusts God for the land instead of grabbing it.
settings.readers: For Israel the story was a lesson for clans and tribes who shared pasture. It also framed Israel's later dealings with Moab and Ammon, Lot's descendants (Deuteronomy 2:9, 19).

settings.what: The promise of the land in every direction
settings.to: Abram, standing near Bethel after Lot has gone east
settings.when: Right after Lot chooses the Plain of the Jordan
settings.why: To give Abram and his offspring all the land he can see, for all time. His offspring will be as many as the dust of the earth, and he is to walk through the land. Looking over land and walking it may have been ways to claim it. The promise answers Lot's choice by sight: Abram receives what he did not grab.
settings.readers: For Israel this was the title deed to Canaan. For exiles it was the promise they held to while the land was in other hands.

title: The Priest-King of Salem
sum: Genesis suddenly turns to world politics. Four kings from the east, led by Chedorlaomer of Elam, crush a revolt by five kings of the Dead Sea cities, sweep through Transjordan, and carry off the goods of Sodom and Gomorrah, and Lot with them. Abram the Hebrew calls out 318 trained men of his household, with his Amorite allies, and in a night attack routs the invaders as far as north of Damascus. He brings back Lot, the people and the goods.

Two kings come out to meet him. Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings bread and wine and blesses him, and Abram gives him a tenth. The king of Sodom offers him the spoil, and Abram refuses even a sandal strap: he has sworn to the LORD, God Most High, that no one but God will make him rich.
readings: Read as history

A raid by eastern overlords to punish rebel vassals, recorded in the style of ancient annals, with old place names explained for later readers ("Bela, that is, Zoar"). Defenders point to the realistic route along the King's Highway and to the coalitions of the Old Babylonian age.
Read as legend or late composition

Many critical scholars find the chapter unlike the rest of Abraham's story: Abram appears as a warlord, the kings are unknown, and the numbers are large. Some date it to the exile or later, as a story written to honor Jerusalem's priesthood through Melchizedek.
Read as a picture of Christ
For Hebrews and the church fathers, Melchizedek is a living picture of Christ: king of righteousness and peace, a priest not from Levi, who blesses Abraham and receives his tithe (Hebrews 7).

views.L: A real campaign about 2000–1800 BC. Abram's small force won by surprise at night, as Gideon later did (Judges 7). Melchizedek was a true worshiper of the one God in Canaan, a remnant of the faith of Noah's family.
views.F: The chapter shows Abram as a blessing to the nations (12:3): he rescues his neighbors, even Sodom. The two kings frame a choice between two kinds of wealth, and Abram chooses blessing from God.
views.C: Chapter 14 fits none of the usual sources (J, E, P) and is often seen as an independent piece, perhaps late. Many think the Melchizedek scene (14:18–20) was added to give the priesthood of Jerusalem, and of David's line (Psalm 110), an ancient pedigree from Abraham.
views.J: The rabbis identified Amraphel with Nimrod, who threw Abram into the furnace, and Melchizedek with Shem, son of Noah (Nedarim 32b). The Talmud says that because Melchizedek blessed Abram before he blessed God, the priesthood was taken from his line and given to Abram's.

deep.h: Melchizedek in the Bible and after
deep.b:
Melchizedek appears in only two passages of the Hebrew Bible. Here he is a real priest-king who blesses Abram. In Psalm 110:4, a royal psalm, God swears to David's lord, "You are a priest forever, after the pattern of Melchizedek." The psalm seems to give Israel's kings in Jerusalem a priestly role inherited from the city's ancient priest-king.

Hebrews builds its whole argument for Christ's priesthood on the two passages (Hebrews 5–7). Jesus came from Judah, not Levi, so he could not be a priest under the Law; but he is a priest like Melchizedek, appointed by God's oath and "by the power of a life that cannot be destroyed" (Hebrews 7:16). Jewish tradition took a different path: Melchizedek was Shem, and his priesthood passed to Abraham. The Dead Sea scroll 11QMelchizedek makes him a heavenly judge and deliverer who will proclaim the final jubilee (Isaiah 61:1–2). Later groups, from some early sects to modern Latter-day Saints, have used his name for orders of priesthood.

The Genesis Apocryphon (1QapGen, column 22), an Aramaic retelling of Genesis found in Cave 1 at Qumran and copied about the first century BC, retells this chapter closely. It says Melchizedek was king of Salem, "that is Jerusalem," and that Abram gave him a tenth of all the goods taken from the king of Elam and his allies.

echoes: Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 5:6–10; Hebrews 6:20; Hebrews 7:1–28; Psalm 76:2; Deuteronomy 2:10–12; Judges 18:29; Numbers 18:21

settings.by: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High
settings.to: Abram, coming back from his victory over the four kings
settings.when: In the Valley of Shaveh, the King's Valley, where the king of Sodom meets Abram
settings.why: To bless Abram by God Most High, maker of heaven and earth, and to bless God for the victory. Abram answers by giving him a tenth.
settings.readers: For Israel, Salem was taken to be Jerusalem (Psalm 76:2), so its own city's priest-king honored their father and received his tithe. Psalm 110:4 promises a king who is a priest like Melchizedek, and Hebrews 7 applies this to Jesus.
views: Many scholars think the story supported the claims of Jerusalem and its kings and priests after David took the city.
Others see an old memory of a Canaanite priest-king taken into the Abraham stories.

settings.what: Abram's oath to the king of Sodom
settings.to: The king of Sodom, who offers him the goods
settings.when: Right after Melchizedek's blessing
settings.why: To refuse any reward from Sodom, not even a thread or a sandal strap, so that no king can say he made Abram rich. Abram has sworn by the LORD, God Most High. He takes only what his men have eaten and his allies' share.
settings.readers: For Israel the lesson was that Abram's wealth must come from God, not from deals with the wicked city of the plain. Melchizedek's blessing and Sodom's offer stand side by side as two kinds of kings.

traditions.q: Did Melchizedek's bread and wine foreshadow the Eucharist as a sacrifice?
views: Yes. Melchizedek's offering of bread and wine prefigures the Eucharist, and the oldest Eucharistic Prayer of the Mass names it (Catechism 1333, 1544). The Council of Trent taught that Christ, a priest in Melchizedek's order, offered his body and blood under bread and wine at the Last Supper and that the Mass makes this one sacrifice present.

The fathers saw the Eucharist in Melchizedek's gifts, and Orthodox liturgy calls the Eucharist a bloodless sacrifice offered by Christ the true high priest. The Orthodox speak of mystery and do not use the Western term transubstantiation.

Luther held that Melchizedek brought out food to refresh Abram's tired men, not a sacrifice to God, and that his priesthood consisted of blessing and teaching. Lutherans believe Christ's body and blood are truly present in the Supper but reject the Mass as a sacrifice offered for sins (Augsburg Confession, article 24).

Calvin read the bread and wine as a meal for soldiers and pointed out that Hebrews, which explains Melchizedek at length, never mentions them. The Supper remembers Christ's one sacrifice, which can never be repeated (Hebrews 7:27; Westminster Confession 29.2).

title: Stars and a Smoking Oven
sum: After the battle, God speaks to Abram in a vision: "Do not be afraid. I am a shield for you." Abram answers with his first recorded complaint: God's gifts mean little while he has no son and a servant will inherit everything. God takes him outside, shows him the night sky, and says his offspring will be as many as the stars. Abram believes, and the LORD counts it to him as righteousness, a sentence that becomes one of the most quoted in the New Testament.

Abram then asks how he can know he will possess the land. God tells him to cut animals in two in the old way of making a covenant. In a deep sleep and great darkness, Abram hears that his descendants will be oppressed in a foreign land for four hundred years and then return. A smoking oven and a blazing torch pass between the pieces: God has bound himself by oath to give the land from Egypt to the Euphrates.
readings: Read as covenant
A formal treaty ceremony, with God alone taking the oath. The chapter is the legal foundation of Israel's claim to the land and the first of God's covenants with Abram (the second is in chapter 17).
Read through Paul
For Paul, 15:6 shows that a person is right with God by trusting his promise, and that this was true before circumcision or the Law (Romans 4; Galatians 3). Abram is the father of all who believe.
Read through Jewish tradition
The rabbis read the "covenant between the pieces" (berit bein habetarim) as the moment when Israel's whole history, slavery, exodus and the four kingdoms, was shown to Abraham in advance.

views.L: Abram really saw this vision about 2000 BC, and the 400 years point exactly to Israel's later stay in Egypt, which ended in the Exodus about 1446 BC (on an early date) or the 1200s BC.
views.F: The chapter has two matching halves: a promise of offspring with a sign (the stars) and a promise of land with a sign (the covenant fire). Each starts with Abram's question and ends with God's answer, teaching that faith can ask honest questions.
views.C: Critical scholars have struggled to divide the chapter among the sources and many now see it as a late composition (perhaps from the 600s or 500s BC) that combines themes of Deuteronomy and the prophets: the word of the LORD, faith, the Exodus, and the land's borders. The prophecy of 400 years is read as written after the events.
views.J: The Mekhilta and later Jewish thought prize 15:6 as the root of Israel's faith. The covenant between the pieces is remembered in the Passover Haggadah: "Blessed is He who keeps his promise to Israel... for the Holy One calculated the end, as he told Abraham our father at the covenant between the pieces," followed by 15:13–14.

deep.h: Faith and righteousness: four readings of 15:6
deep.b:
Paul. Abram was counted righteous before he was circumcised (chapter 17) and centuries before the Law, so righteousness comes to all who share his faith, Jews and Gentiles (Romans 4:9–17; Galatians 3:6–9). The Reformers read this as justification by faith alone: God credits Christ's righteousness to the believer. The "New Perspective on Paul" (E. P. Sanders, James Dunn, N. T. Wright) argues that the "works of the Law" Paul rejects are mainly the markers of Jewish identity, such as circumcision and food laws, so Romans 4 is chiefly about who belongs to Abraham's family.

James. James reads "reckoned" in the light of chapter 22: Abraham's faith "worked together with his works" when he offered Isaac, and "a person is made right by works and not by faith alone" (James 2:21–24). Paul stresses that chapter 15 comes before chapter 17; James that it is completed in chapter 22. Many scholars think they answer different questions.

Catholic and Orthodox teaching. The Council of Trent (Session 6, 1547, chapter 8 and canon 9) taught that faith is the beginning of justification but not faith alone apart from hope and love. Orthodox theology speaks of faith working through love (Galatians 5:6). In 1999 Lutherans and Catholics signed the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification, agreeing that "by grace alone, in faith" a person is accepted by God.

Jewish tradition. Faith (emunah) is trust and faithfulness together. 1 Maccabees 2:52 asks, "Abraham: was he not found faithful in the test, and was it not reckoned to him as righteousness?" The Mekhilta says Abraham inherited this world and the next as the reward of his trust.

Woolley's excavations at Ur (1922–1934) uncovered the Royal Cemetery, with the famous "Standard of Ur" and the "Ram in a Thicket" statues (about 2600 BC), now in the British Museum and the Penn Museum. Woolley believed he had found Abraham's city, but nothing found there mentions Abraham.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the night of the stars and the night of the oven
deep.body: An observation of my own: the chapter happens across two dark scenes. In the first, Abram is taken outside to see the stars, which means it is night (15:5); yet 15:12 says the sun is only going down. Many solve this by placing the two halves on different days. I suspect the narrator wants the reader to feel both darkness and light as signs: the stars as the promise's light in the dark, and the "great darkness" as the dark years of Egypt, which only God's own fire passes through. The two signs answer Abram's two questions.

echoes: Romans 4:1–25; Galatians 3:6–18; James 2:21–23; Hebrews 6:13–18; Hebrews 11:8–12; Jeremiah 34:18–20; Exodus 12:40–41; Acts 7:6–7; Nehemiah 9:7–8

settings.what: The promise of a son and the stars
settings.by: The LORD, in a vision, with Abram's complaint
settings.to: Abram, still childless after the battle
settings.when: Some time after the war of the kings
settings.why: To answer Abram's fear and his complaint that a servant will be his heir. A son from his own body will inherit, and his offspring will be as many as the stars. Abram trusts the LORD, and the LORD counts it to him as righteousness.
settings.readers: For Israel the scene taught that the nation itself was a gift to a man who could only believe. Paul builds his teaching on faith on this verse (Romans 4; Galatians 3:6), and James uses it in another way (James 2:23).
views: Paul and the Protestant tradition read 15:6 as God counting Abram's trust as right standing.
Many Jewish readers, and some Christians, read it as faithfulness that God honors. Ramban suggests that Abram counted God's promise as God's righteousness.

settings.to: Abram, after he asks how he will know he will possess the land
settings.when: At sunset and in the dark, after Abram has cut the animals in two
settings.why: To guarantee the land by an oath. In an old rite the parties walked between cut animals, calling the same fate on themselves if they broke faith (Jeremiah 34:18). Here only God passes through, as a smoking oven and a blazing torch: he alone binds himself. He also tells Abram the future. His offspring will be foreigners and slaves for four hundred years, God will judge that nation, and they will come back in the fourth generation.
settings.readers: For Israel the words explained the slavery in Egypt before it happened. They also explained the long delay in receiving the land, since "the guilt of the Amorites is not yet full" (15:16).
views: Moshe Weinfeld compared royal land grants in which a king binds himself by oath to a loyal servant.

Many critical scholars note that the borders from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates match the ideal reach of Solomon's kingdom (1 Kings 4:21). They think the prophecy was shaped by people who knew the exodus story.

traditions.q: When God counted Abram's trust as righteousness (15:6), what did justification mean?
views: God justifies freely, for Christ's sake, through faith, which he counts as righteousness, as Paul argues from this verse in Romans 4 (Augsburg Confession, article 4). Good works follow faith, but they add nothing to a person's standing before God.

Justification is a legal act: God pardons sins and counts believers righteous because Christ's obedience is credited to them, not because a new righteousness is put inside them (Westminster Confession 11.1). Faith alone receives it, though true faith is never alone but always works by love.

Justification is both forgiveness and the inner renewal of the person, as God's grace makes the believer truly righteous (Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 7; Catechism 1987–1995). Faith begins it, joined with hope and love. In 1999 Catholics and Lutherans declared that they agree on the basic truths, though some differences remain.

The Orthodox rarely frame salvation in the legal terms of the Western debate. Justification is part of one life of union with God, in which faith works through love (Galatians 5:6) and the believer is slowly made holy.

Wesley preached justification by faith alone as firmly as Luther, but stressed that the new birth begins at the same moment and must grow into holiness of heart and life. The World Methodist Council joined the 1999 Joint Declaration in 2006.

title: The God Who Sees
sum: Ten years after the call, Sarai is still childless. She turns to an accepted custom of her world: she gives her Egyptian slave Hagar to Abram as a second wife, hoping to gain a son through her. Hagar conceives and begins to look down on Sarai. Sarai blames Abram, Abram hands Hagar back to her, and Sarai mistreats her until she runs away into the wilderness on the road to Egypt.

At a desert spring, the angel of the LORD finds her. He tells her to go back, but promises her countless descendants and a son named Ishmael, "God hears," a free and fierce man of the desert. Hagar, a foreign slave woman, gives God a name of her own: El-roi, "God who sees." She returns, and Abram, at eighty-six, names his firstborn son.
readings: Read as family drama
A story of rivalry between two women in a household built on one man's need for an heir, told without heroes. Each person acts in a way their world allowed, and each one is hurt.
Read as Hagar's story

Told from below, it is the story of a foreign slave who is used, mistreated and then met by God in the desert. Phyllis Trible counted it among the Bible's "texts of terror," and Delores Williams made Hagar a model for Black women's survival and faith.
Read through Paul
For Paul, Hagar's son was "born according to the flesh," by human planning, while Isaac was born "through the promise" (Galatians 4:23). The story becomes an allegory of two covenants (see 21:10).

views.L: A real event about 2080 BC by a literal count. Hagar's son Ishmael was the real ancestor of Arab tribes, as Genesis 25:12–18 records.
views.F: The chapter mirrors the Exodus in reverse: an Egyptian slave is oppressed by Hebrews, flees into the wilderness, and is met by God at a spring, who "hears" her misery. Israel's readers are invited to see the oppressed from the other side.
views.C: Mostly from J, with P's framework of ages in 16:1a, 3 and 15–16. Many scholars see an older story of a tribal ancestor (Ishmael) and a desert well, retold to explain Israel's ties with Arab neighbors.
views.J: The Midrash made Hagar Pharaoh's daughter, and one tradition identifies her with Keturah, whom Abraham later marries (25:1; Genesis Rabbah 61:4; Rashi). Ramban criticized both Sarai and Abram for their treatment of her.

deep.b:
The Qur'an does not tell Hagar's story by name, but it has Abraham pray after settling "some of my offspring in a valley without crops, near your sacred House" (Qur'an 14:37). The hadith collection of al-Bukhari tells the fuller story: Abraham left Hagar and the infant Ishmael in the valley of Mecca with a waterskin; when it ran dry she ran seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa looking for help, until an angel (in some reports, Gabriel) struck the ground and the spring of Zamzam burst out. Every Muslim pilgrim repeats her run in the ritual called the sa'y.

Islamic tradition places these events in Arabia, not in the Negev. Historians see the Islamic accounts as developing from the biblical story and Arab traditions (Reuven Firestone traces this growth in Journeys in Holy Lands). For Muslims they are the true account of a woman whose faith God honored.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the three names of chapter 16
deep.body: My own reading: the chapter turns on three acts of naming that move from heaven to earth. The angel names the child Ishmael, "God hears" (16:11). Hagar names God El-roi, "God sees" (16:13). And Abram names the son (16:15), the only thing he does in the chapter apart from obeying Sarai. Hearing and seeing are exactly what God does for Israel in Egypt: "I have seen, yes seen, the suffering of my people... I have heard their outcry" (Exodus 3:7). The slave from Egypt receives in advance what Israel will receive in Egypt.

settings.by: The angel of the LORD, and Hagar's reply
settings.to: Hagar, Sarai's Egyptian slave, pregnant and running away
settings.when: At a spring in the desert on the road to Shur, toward Egypt
settings.why: To send her back to her mistress, and to promise her more offspring than can be counted. Her son will be named Ishmael, "God hears," and will live free in the desert. A foreign slave woman receives a promise like Abram's. She gives God a name of her own, El-roi, "God who sees," and the well is named for it.
settings.readers: For Israel, a people of former slaves in Egypt, God sees an Egyptian slave in her misery. The desert tribes of Arabia were counted as Ishmael's sons (25:12–18), so Israel's neighbors too had a place in God's care.

title: A New Name and a Sign
sum: Thirteen years pass in silence. When Abram is ninety-nine, God appears as El Shaddai, God Almighty, and lays out his covenant in full. Abram's name becomes Abraham, "father of a multitude of nations." God promises nations and kings from him, the whole land of Canaan for all time, and above all, "I will be God to you and to your offspring after you."

Abraham's part is to keep the covenant, and its sign is to be cut in the flesh: every male of his household, slave and free, is to be circumcised, and every son on his eighth day. Sarai becomes Sarah, and God promises that she, at ninety, will bear the son of the covenant. Abraham falls on his face and laughs, and pleads for Ishmael. God blesses Ishmael with twelve chiefs, but names the coming son Isaac. That same day, Abraham and every male of his house are circumcised.
readings: Read as law
The founding text of circumcision for the Jewish people, still read at every brit milah. It defines who belongs to Abraham's covenant household, including foreign-born slaves.
Read as promise
The chapter is mostly God speaking: names, nations, kings, land, and "I will be their God." Abraham's only words are a laugh and a prayer for the son he already has.
Read through Paul
Paul notes the order: Abraham was counted righteous in chapter 15 and circumcised in chapter 17, so circumcision is a seal of faith he already had (Romans 4:9–12).

views.L: A real appearance of God to Abraham in his ninety-ninth year, and the historical beginning of circumcision as Israel's covenant sign.
views.F: The chapter echoes creation: "Be fruitful and grow many" (1:28) becomes "I will make you fruitful beyond measure" (17:6). God's renaming of Abram and Sarai, like his naming in Genesis 1, creates something new.
views.C: Almost all critical scholars assign this chapter to the Priestly source (P): it uses "God" (Elohim) and El Shaddai, speaks of an "everlasting covenant," counts ages, and stresses a ritual sign. Many date P to the exile or just after, when circumcision and the Sabbath became key marks of Jewish identity far from the land.
views.J: The rabbis say Abraham became "whole" (17:1) only through circumcision (Genesis Rabbah 46). The Talmud holds that whoever calls him "Abram" breaks a commandment. The chapter is part of the Torah portion Lekh Lekha, and its words are recited at every circumcision.

deep.b:
Chapters 15 and 17 both describe God making a covenant with Abraham. In chapter 15 God alone swears, by passing between the pieces, and the focus is land. In chapter 17 God "establishes" his covenant, gives it a sign, and asks Abraham to keep it; the focus is offspring and God's relation to them. Some readers see two stages of one covenant; others see two covenants; critical scholars usually see two sources (an older or non-Priestly one in chapter 15 and P in chapter 17). After the binding of Isaac, God adds an oath (22:16–18).

Christian theology has drawn on these chapters for "covenant theology," which sees one covenant of grace running from Abraham to Christ, and for dispensational theology, which stresses the land promises to ethnic Israel as still in force.

At a Jewish circumcision the baby is placed on a chair called the "Chair of Elijah," and those present answer the father's blessing: "Just as he has entered the covenant, so may he enter into Torah, into marriage, and into good deeds." The ceremony is called "the covenant of Abraham our father" (brit Avraham avinu).

echoes: Romans 4:9–21; Galatians 3:15–18; Galatians 5:2–6; Acts 7:8; Acts 15:1–21; Colossians 2:11–12; Exodus 6:2–8; Leviticus 12:3; Jeremiah 4:4; Revelation 21:3

settings.by: God, as El Shaddai, God Almighty
settings.to: Abram, at ninety-nine
settings.when: Thirteen years after Ishmael's birth
settings.why: To set out God's side of the covenant in full. Abram becomes Abraham, father of a multitude of nations. Kings will come from him, and the land of Canaan will be his offspring's to hold forever. Above all, "I will be God to you and to your offspring after you" (17:7).
settings.readers: For Israel under its kings, and in exile without a king, the promise of kings was older than David. The covenant was "forever," so the loss of land and throne could not end it.

settings.to: Abraham, for himself, his household and his offspring generation after generation
settings.when: In the same speech, after God's promises
settings.why: To give the covenant a sign in the flesh. It binds every male of Abraham's household: sons on their eighth day, slaves born in the house, and slaves bought from foreigners. A male who is not circumcised is cut off from his people. The problem it answers is belonging: how a family marks who is inside God's covenant.
settings.readers: For Israel the law applied to every boy in every generation, wherever they lived (Leviticus 12:3). Neighboring peoples circumcised boys near puberty or marriage; the eighth day made it a mark received, not earned. In exile, with no temple and no land, circumcision and the Sabbath became the chief signs of being a Jew.
views: Traditional readers take it as God's command to Abraham, repeated for every Israelite boy in Leviticus 12:3.
Many critical scholars assign the chapter to the Priestly source (P) and see it speaking to exiles who needed a sign of identity among foreign peoples.
Scholars who date P before the exile (Kaufmann, Milgrom) read it as the law of Israel in its own land.

The prophets and Paul read the sign as calling for a changed heart (Deuteronomy 10:16; Jeremiah 4:4; Romans 2:28–29). Paul notes that Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised (Romans 4:9–12).

settings.to: Abraham, about Sarai his wife and about Ishmael
settings.when: In the same speech
settings.why: To rename Sarai as Sarah and promise that she, at ninety, will bear the son of the covenant, Isaac, within a year. Abraham laughs and pleads for Ishmael. God blesses Ishmael with twelve chieftains but keeps the covenant for Isaac.
settings.readers: For Israel the words taught that its line came from God's gift, not from human planning (16:2). They also honored Ishmael's line, Israel's desert neighbors, even as they set it aside.

traditions.q: Does circumcision on the eighth day mean that infants should be baptized?
views: Baptism is the circumcision of Christ (Colossians 2:11–12) and the door into the new covenant, and the Church has baptized infants from the earliest times because it washes away original sin and gives new life by grace that no one earns (Catechism 1250–1252, 527).
Infants are baptized, anointed with chrism and given communion in the same service, and they belong fully to the church from that day.

Children should be baptized, because God offers his grace through baptism (Augsburg Confession, article 9). For Lutherans baptism is God's own work and promise, which gives new birth and which faith later trusts.

As circumcision marked Abraham's children as members of the covenant, baptism marks the children of believers (Heidelberg Catechism Q74; Westminster Confession 28.4). It is a sign and seal of God's promise, not something that saves by itself.

Baptism is only for those who confess faith in Christ, by immersion (1689 Confession 29.2, 29.4; Baptist Faith and Message, article 7). Circumcision marked a physical nation, but in the new covenant every member knows the Lord (Jeremiah 31:34), and circumcision of the heart takes its place.

The first Anabaptists baptized one another as adults in Zurich in 1525 and were persecuted for it by Catholics and Protestants alike. The Schleitheim Confession (1527) gives baptism to those who have learned repentance and asked for it themselves.

title: Guests at Mamre
sum: In the noonday heat, the LORD appears to Abraham as three travelers. Abraham runs to meet them, bows, and offers water and a bit of bread, then serves a feast: fresh bread from over five gallons of flour, a tender calf, curds and milk. The guests ask for Sarah, and one of them promises she will have a son by this time next year. Sarah, listening behind the tent door, laughs to herself. "Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?"

As the visitors look down toward Sodom, the LORD tells Abraham what he is about to do: the outcry from Sodom and Gomorrah is great, and he will go down and see. Abraham stands before the LORD and argues: "Will the Judge of all the earth not do what is just?" Step by step he bargains, from fifty righteous people down to ten. Each time, God agrees.
readings: Read as a story of hospitality

The chapter is the Bible's great picture of welcoming strangers, which Hebrews urges on its readers (Hebrews 13:2). It sets up a deliberate contrast with Sodom's treatment of the same visitors in chapter 19.
Read as theophany

God himself comes to eat at a man's table and talks with him as a friend. Christians have seen in the scene a foreshadowing of the Incarnation, or of the Trinity; Jews see God's closeness to the righteous.
Read as a debate about justice

The second half asks whether God's justice can tell the innocent from the guilty, and whether a few good people can save many. The question is never fully closed; chapter 19 gives God's answer in action.

views.L: God really appeared in human form with two angels and ate with Abraham, and Abraham really pleaded with him. Many traditional Christians identify the LORD here as the Son of God before his incarnation.
views.F: The chapter pairs two scenes at two tents: a meal where God promises life, and a walk where God speaks of death. Both turn on a question: "Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?" and "Will the Judge of all the earth not do what is just?" The reader learns God's power and his justice together.
views.C: Assigned to J. Many scholars think an old story of gods visiting a hospitable old couple lies behind it, like the Greek tale of Baucis and Philemon (told by Ovid), and that 18:17–33 is a later, more reflective addition about God's justice, perhaps from the time after Jerusalem fell, when people asked whether the righteous had died with the wicked.
views.J: For the rabbis this chapter is the model of hakhnasat orchim, welcoming guests, and of bikkur cholim, visiting the sick. A well-known Jewish tradition says Abraham's tent had openings on all four sides so he could see travelers coming from any direction.

deep.title: Gods who visit in disguise
deep.b: In Ovid's Metamorphoses (book 8), Jupiter and Mercury, disguised as travelers, are turned away by every house in a town except that of an old poor couple, Baucis and Philemon, who serve them a meal. The gods flood the town and save the couple. The likeness to Genesis 18–19 is real: hospitality to disguised divine guests, an old couple, and the destruction of an inhospitable place. But Ovid wrote around AD 8, long after Genesis, and the theme of testing hospitality is common in many cultures. Most scholars see a shared motif, not borrowing. Acts 14:11–12 shows the people of Lystra assuming that Paul and Barnabas were Zeus and Hermes come down in human form, a sign the idea was alive in that region.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Abraham bargains like a merchant because he was one
deep.body: A small observation of my own: the bargaining in 18:24–32 follows the steps of a Near Eastern market, as Abraham's purchase of the cave in chapter 23 also does, with humble words ("I am only dust and ashes"), a polite pretense of not wanting to push, and steady reductions. The narrator may want us to see Abraham using the ordinary skills of a wealthy trader for the sake of strangers. Whether or not that is so, the reversal is striking: in chapter 23 Abraham pays a full price for a grave; here he bargains God down for the sake of life.

echoes: Hebrews 13:2; Romans 9:9; Luke 1:37; 1 Peter 3:6; James 2:23; Isaiah 41:8; Ezekiel 16:49–50; Jeremiah 5:1; Exodus 32:11–14; Matthew 13:33

settings.by: The LORD, as one of the three visitors
settings.to: Abraham, while Sarah listens at the tent door
settings.when: At the meal under the great trees of Mamre
settings.why: To fix the time: Sarah will have a son when the season comes round. Sarah laughs to herself, and the LORD asks, "Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?"
settings.readers: For Israel, which owed its existence to this birth, the question was meant for every time of impossible need. Luke echoes it when the angel tells Mary that nothing is impossible for God (Luke 1:37).

settings.what: The LORD's thoughts about Abraham and Sodom
settings.to: No one in the story; the narrator lets the readers listen in
settings.when: As the visitors look down toward Sodom
settings.why: To explain why God shares his plan with Abraham. Abraham has been chosen to teach his children and household to keep the LORD's way by doing what is right and fair. The outcry against Sodom will be checked before judgment falls.
settings.readers: For Israel the speech defined its calling as a people of justice. It also showed a God who does not punish on rumor.

settings.to: The LORD, before whom Abraham is still standing (18:22)
settings.when: After the two men leave for Sodom
settings.why: To argue that the Judge of all the earth must not sweep away the righteous with the wicked. Abraham bargains from fifty down to ten. He learns that God's mercy is wider than the bargain: God would spare the whole city for ten.
settings.readers: For Israel the scene was a model of a prophet's pleading, like Moses for the people (Exodus 32:11–14). It also raised the question of shared guilt, which Ezekiel 18 takes up for the exiles.
views: The Hebrew and the Plain say that Abraham stood before the LORD.
A rabbinic tradition lists 18:22 among the "corrections of the scribes" and holds that the text once said the LORD stood before Abraham, a wording changed out of reverence.

title: Fire on the Cities of the Plain
sum: Two angels reach Sodom at evening. Lot, sitting at the city gate, insists they stay with him and bakes them a meal. Before they can sleep, every man of the city surrounds the house and demands the guests be brought out to be raped. Lot steps outside, pleads, and offers his virgin daughters instead. The crowd turns on him. The angels pull him inside and strike the mob with blinding light.

At dawn the angels drag Lot, his wife and two daughters out of the city; his future sons-in-law think he is joking. Lot begs to flee to the little town of Zoar instead of the hills. Then the LORD rains sulfur and fire and overthrows the cities and the plain. Lot's wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. Abraham, at the place where he had pleaded, sees smoke rising like a kiln. Hiding in a cave, Lot's daughters get their father drunk and conceive by him the ancestors of Moab and Ammon.
readings: Read as history
A real destruction of cities in the Dead Sea basin, remembered in detail. Traditional readers and some archaeologists look for its traces at Bab edh-Dhra or Tall el-Hammam.
Read as a story about hospitality

The chapter is the dark mirror of chapter 18. Abraham welcomes strangers; Sodom tries to violate them. The city's sin is shown, not just named, and its judgment is the answer to Abraham's question about justice.
Read as the Bible's pattern of judgment

Sodom becomes the standard example of sudden judgment throughout Scripture (Isaiah 1:9; Amos 4:11; Luke 17:28–32; 2 Peter 2:6; Jude 7), and Lot's rescue the pattern of God saving the righteous out of it.

views.L: The cities were real and the fire was a real judgment of God, possibly using natural means. Lot's wife was truly turned into a salt pillar, as the Wisdom of Solomon and Josephus believed.
views.F: The chapter is built in contrasts with chapter 18: evening instead of noon, a city instead of a tent, a mob instead of a host, daughters offered instead of a son promised. Its point is moral and theological: God hears the cry of the victims and judges.
views.C: Mostly J, with 19:29 from P. Many critical scholars see a local legend explaining the Dead Sea's desolate landscape, its salt formations and the origins of Moab and Ammon, joined to the Abraham cycle.
views.J: The rabbis portrayed Sodom as a city whose laws forbade charity and tormented strangers, with a famous "bed of Sodom" to which guests were stretched or cut to fit (Sanhedrin 109b). The Mishnah calls the attitude "what is mine is mine and what is yours is yours" "the trait of Sodom" (Avot 5:10).

deep.h: Sodom in the rest of the Bible
deep.b: No city is mentioned more often as a warning. Moses warns that a disobedient Israel's land will become "like the overthrow of Sodom" (Deuteronomy 29:23). Isaiah calls Jerusalem's rulers "rulers of Sodom" and says that if God had not left a few survivors, "we would have been like Sodom" (Isaiah 1:9–10). Ezekiel says Jerusalem was worse than Sodom, whose sin was "pride, more food than they needed, and easy comfort," neglect of the poor, and "a detestable thing" (Ezekiel 16:46–50). Jesus says the towns that reject his message will fare worse than Sodom (Matthew 10:15) and compares his coming to the day fire fell on it (Luke 17:28–30). Peter and Jude use Sodom as a pattern of judgment on the ungodly (2 Peter 2:6; Jude 7).

Bab edh-Dhra, on the Lisan peninsula of the Dead Sea in Jordan, was a walled Early Bronze Age town with an enormous cemetery, perhaps holding tens of thousands of burials. Its town was abandoned about 2350 BC; nearby Numeira was destroyed earlier, about 2600–2550 BC, on the dates of the excavators. Walter Rast and R. Thomas Schaub, who excavated them, were cautious about linking them to Sodom and Gomorrah; others, such as Bryant Wood, have argued for the link.

The Mishnah (Avot 5:10) lists four kinds of people. The one who says "What is mine is mine and what is yours is yours" is called average, but "some say this is the trait of Sodom": a society where no one harms anyone, but no one helps anyone either. Jewish law has a principle called kofin al middat Sedom, "we compel a person not to act in the manner of Sodom," used to stop someone from refusing a favor that costs him nothing.

echoes: Judges 19:15–30; Deuteronomy 29:23; Isaiah 1:9–10; Ezekiel 16:46–50; Amos 4:11; Matthew 10:15; Luke 17:28–33; 2 Peter 2:6–9; Jude 7

settings.what: The men of Sodom and Lot at the door
settings.by: The men of Sodom, then Lot
settings.to: Lot at his door; then the crowd of men from every quarter of the city
settings.when: The night the two guests arrive, before they go to bed
settings.why: The men of the city demand that Lot bring out his guests "so we can know them." Lot pleads with them not to do this evil and offers his two daughters instead, because the men have come under his roof. The crowd turns on him as a foreigner who plays judge. The speeches prove the outcry against Sodom (18:20–21) true.
settings.readers: For Israel the scene made Sodom the byword for a wicked city. Judges 19:22–24 tells a nearly identical scene at Gibeah, to show Israel become like Sodom. Ezekiel 16:49 names Sodom's pride, plenty and neglect of the poor.
views: Many scholars (Bailey) stress the attempted gang rape of strangers and the breach of hospitality as the heart of the sin.
Others (Gagnon), with much Jewish and Christian tradition and Jude 7, see same-sex intercourse as part of the sin as well as the violence.

settings.by: The two angels, with Lot's pleas
settings.to: Lot and his family, in his house in Sodom
settings.when: The night of the attack on his house, and at dawn
settings.why: To get Lot out before the city is destroyed: gather your family, run for your life, and do not look back. Lot's sons-in-law think he is joking. Lot lingers and bargains for the little town of Zoar, and his wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. The rescue is an act of the LORD's pity (19:16), not Lot's merit.
settings.readers: For Israel the story warned against clinging to a doomed place. Jesus tells his disciples to remember Lot's wife (Luke 17:32).

title: A Prophet in Gerar
sum: Abraham moves to Gerar in the western Negev and once again says of Sarah, "She is my sister." King Abimelech takes her, but before he touches her God comes to him in a dream: "You are a dead man." Abimelech protests his innocence, and God agrees, but orders him to return Sarah, "He is a prophet, and he will pray for you."

In the morning the king confronts Abraham: "What have you done to us?" Abraham explains that he thought there was no fear of God in the place, and that Sarah is in fact his half-sister. Abimelech returns Sarah with flocks, slaves and a thousand pieces of silver, and invites Abraham to live anywhere in his land. Abraham prays, and God heals the king's household, whose wombs had been closed.
readings: Read as a second test
Just before the promised son is born, the promise is put at risk again. If Sarah had remained in Abimelech's house, whose son would Isaac be? The story removes every doubt about Isaac's father.
Read as a story about outsiders
The pagan king fears God, argues for justice, and behaves more honorably than the prophet. Genesis repeatedly shows God at work among the nations, and Abraham learning that.

views.L: A real second event, which Abraham himself explains as part of a long-standing plan (20:13). The repetition shows human weakness, not a duplicated source.
views.F: Compared with 12:10–20, this version is more concerned with guilt and innocence: God speaks, Abimelech argues, and the narrator makes sure we know the king never touched Sarah. Abraham's lie is half true, and his role as prophet is underlined.
views.C: Classically assigned to the Elohist (E), the source that calls God "Elohim," prefers dreams to direct appearances, and is more concerned with morality. Many scholars now doubt that E ever existed as a separate document and see this chapter as a deliberate retelling of 12:10–20.
views.J: The rabbis held that God appears to the nations only at night in dreams, but to Israel's prophets openly (Genesis Rabbah). They praised Abimelech's fear of God, and drew from 20:17 and 21:1 the lesson that praying for others brings one's own answer.

settings.by: God, in a dream at night
settings.to: Abimelech, king of Gerar, who has taken Sarah
settings.when: Before he has touched her
settings.why: To warn the king that he is a dead man for taking another man's wife, and to accept his plea of a clear heart. God himself kept him from sinning. Abraham is called a prophet who will pray for him. The foreign king fears God more than Abraham thought (20:11).
settings.readers: For Israel the lesson was that the nations, too, live under God's moral law. God keeps his promise even when its bearer fails.

title: Laughter, and a Well in the Desert
sum: At last the LORD does for Sarah what he promised. At a hundred, Abraham has a son, names him Isaac, "he laughs," and circumcises him on the eighth day. Sarah says, "God has made laughter for me." But at the feast for Isaac's weaning, Sarah sees Ishmael "laughing" and demands that Abraham drive out the slave woman and her son. Abraham is distressed until God tells him to listen to Sarah, and promises that Ishmael too will become a nation.

Early in the morning Abraham sends Hagar and the boy away with bread and a skin of water. In the wilderness of Beersheba the water runs out; Hagar leaves the boy under a bush and sits a bowshot away so she will not watch him die. God hears the boy's voice, the angel calls from heaven, and God opens her eyes to a well. Ishmael grows up an archer in the wilderness of Paran. Meanwhile Abraham makes a treaty with Abimelech at Beersheba, the "well of the oath," plants a tamarisk, and calls on the Everlasting God.
readings: Read as the promise kept
After twenty-five years and many threats, the son arrives "at the very time God had told him." The chapter is the turning point of Abraham's story; what remains is the test of that son (chapter 22).
Read as Ishmael's story

Half the chapter follows the rejected son and his mother. God hears, provides and blesses them too. Jewish tradition reads it at the New Year; Muslims remember the same mother and son as founders of Mecca's holy places.
Read through Paul
Paul reads Sarah's demand as Scripture's word that the children of promise, not of slavery, inherit (Galatians 4:21–31).

views.L: Isaac was born about 2066 BC on the traditional count (or a little later), and the events at Beersheba really happened. The Philistine name may be a later scribe's update.
views.F: The chapter is built on laughter: Sarah's joy, Ishmael's "laughing," Abraham's grief turned to God's assurance. The expulsion of Hagar mirrors the binding of Isaac that follows: two sons, two mornings, two rescues from heaven.
views.C: 21:1–5 is mostly P (ages, circumcision); 21:6–21 and 21:22–34 are usually assigned to E, which here prefers "God" and the "angel of God." The Philistines and the treaty at Beersheba are taken as signs of a writer in the time of Israel's kings.
views.J: Genesis 21 is read on the first day of Rosh Hashanah. The rabbis noticed that God "took note of" Sarah (21:1) and said that on the New Year God remembered Sarah, Rachel and Hannah (Rosh Hashanah 11a). They also taught that God judged Ishmael "as he was then," not for his descendants' future deeds.

deep.h: Ishmael in Jewish, Christian and Muslim tradition
deep.b:
Jewish tradition is mixed. Some rabbis made Ishmael a mocker or idolater; others said he repented, pointing out that at Abraham's burial he let Isaac go first (25:9; Bava Batra 16b; Rashi on 25:9). In later Jewish writing "Ishmael" became a name for the Arab peoples.

Christian tradition has mostly followed Paul's allegory (Galatians 4), sometimes harshly, though Genesis itself stresses that God was "with the boy" (21:20).

Islam honors Isma'il as a prophet and as the son who helped Abraham raise the foundations of the Kaaba in Mecca (Qur'an 2:127). Many Muslim scholars hold that he, not Isaac, was the son Abraham was ready to sacrifice (see 22:2). The pilgrimage rites of the hajj recall Hagar's search for water, Abraham's sacrifice and the stoning of the devil who tempted him.

deep.title: Claude's theory: two sons, one laughter
deep.body: My own reading, building on observations by Wenham and others: the narrator seems to make a pun of 21:9. Sarah sees Ishmael metsacheq, "laughing" or "Isaac-ing." The boy who is not Isaac is doing what Isaac's name means. Sarah's fear may be that Ishmael is taking the place and the role of the promised child. If so, the conflict is not about a single act of cruelty but about who carries the name of the promise. God answers by giving each son his own future: one the covenant, the other a great nation and a well in the desert.

echoes: Galatians 4:21–31; Romans 9:6–9; Hebrews 11:11–12; Hebrews 11:17–18; 1 Samuel 2:1–10; 26:26–33; Isaiah 54:1

settings.to: Everyone who will hear of Isaac's birth
settings.when: After Isaac is born and circumcised
settings.why: To turn her laughter of doubt (18:12) into laughter of joy, and to invite others to laugh with her. The name Isaac means "he laughs."
settings.readers: For Israel, the people that came from Isaac, the little poem made its own beginning a joke of God's grace. A mother too old to bear became a mother of nations.

settings.what: God's word about Hagar and Ishmael
settings.to: Abraham, troubled by Sarah's demand to send them away
settings.when: At the feast for Isaac's weaning
settings.why: To tell Abraham to listen to Sarah, because his offspring will be named through Isaac. God also promises that Ishmael will become a nation. The words ease Abraham's grief and put limits on a harsh scene.
settings.readers: For Israel this explained how the line of promise ran through Isaac without making Ishmael's people cursed. Paul uses the story as an allegory of two covenants (Galatians 4:21–31).

settings.what: The angel's words to Hagar in the desert
settings.by: The angel of God, calling from the sky
settings.to: Hagar, sitting a bowshot away from her dying son
settings.when: In the wilderness of Beersheba, when the water runs out
settings.why: To tell her not to be afraid, because God has heard the boy's voice, and to promise that he will be a great nation. Then God opens her eyes to a well. As in 16:11, God hears the outcast.
settings.readers: For Israel this was a reminder that God's care reaches beyond the chosen line. Israel too would later cry from a wilderness and be given water (Exodus 17:1–7).

settings.by: Abimelech, with his commander Phicol, and Abraham
settings.to: Each other, as heads of their households and peoples
settings.when: Some time after Hagar is sent away
settings.why: To make a treaty. Abraham swears not to betray Abimelech's family. Abimelech accepts seven ewe lambs as a witness that Abraham dug the well. The place is named Beersheba, "well of the oath" or "well of seven."
settings.readers: For Israel this was a claim to the wells of the Negev and a model of peace with neighbors in the land. Isaac's treaty in 26:26–31 repeats it.
views: Traditional scholars note how such disputes over wells and treaties fit the life of herders in the second millennium BC.
Many critical scholars point out that the Philistines are not known in Canaan before about 1175 BC, so the name reflects the time of the writer.

title: The Binding of Isaac
sum: "Some time after these things, God put Abraham to the test." The test is the worst a father could imagine: take your son, your only one, whom you love, Isaac, and offer him as a burnt offering on a mountain in the land of Moriah. Abraham says nothing. He rises early, saddles his donkey, splits wood, and walks three days. He lays the wood on Isaac and carries the fire and the knife, and the two walk on together. "Where is the lamb?" asks Isaac. "God will see to the lamb for himself, my son."

Abraham builds the altar, binds his son and lifts the knife. The angel of the LORD calls from heaven: stop. "Now I know that you fear God." Abraham sees a ram caught by its horns and offers it in place of his son, and names the place "The LORD Will See." Then God swears by himself to bless him and to bless all nations through his offspring. Abraham returns to Beersheba, and news comes from Nahor's family, among them a girl named Rebekah.
readings: Read as a test of faith

The traditional Jewish and Christian reading: Abraham trusts that God will keep his promise through Isaac even if it means death, and God never meant him to kill the boy. Hebrews says Abraham believed God could raise the dead (Hebrews 11:19).
Read as a picture of Christ

The beloved son carries the wood up a hill, is laid on it as a sacrifice, and is "received back" on the third day. But here a ram dies instead; at Calvary, Christians say, God himself provided the Lamb and did not spare his own Son (Romans 8:32).
Read as a protest against child sacrifice
Some scholars read the story as ending a practice: the God of Israel does not want children burned, as Israel's neighbors did, and the ram replaces the son forever (Jeremiah 7:31).

views.L: A real event on the hill where the Temple later stood (2 Chronicles 3:1). Isaac was probably a young man, strong enough to carry the wood, and submitted willingly.
views.F: The story is a masterpiece of spare narration: few words, no feelings named, repeated phrases ("the two of them walked on together," "Here I am") and the key verb "see" (22:4, 8, 13, 14). It closes Abraham's story of faith that began with the same words "go for yourself" (12:1; 22:2).
views.C: Traditionally assigned to E (using "God"), with 22:15–18 widely seen as a later addition that turns the story into a basis for the promises. Many scholars see an old tale explaining a sanctuary's name, or the replacement of child sacrifice by animal sacrifice, reshaped into a story of obedience.
views.J: The Akedah is central to Jewish prayer and memory: it is read on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, recalled in the daily morning prayers, and invoked through the shofar. The rabbis saw Isaac as a willing adult, and Jews in times of persecution saw their martyrs as new Isaacs.

deep.b:
Judaism. The story is called the Akedah, the Binding. The rabbis said that God remembers it on behalf of Israel ("the merit of the fathers"), and the morning prayers include it daily. After the massacres of Rhineland Jews in 1096, poets wrote that Jewish parents had done what Abraham was spared from doing; Shalom Spiegel's The Last Trial traces that history.

Christianity. The New Testament draws on it lightly but clearly: "He who did not hold back his own Son" (Romans 8:32, echoing Genesis 22:16 in Greek), the "beloved Son" (Mark 1:11), and Hebrews' reading of Abraham's faith in resurrection (Hebrews 11:17–19). Church fathers such as Melito of Sardis, Origen and Augustine developed the comparison between Isaac and Christ, with the ram as Christ caught in the thorns.

Islam. In the Qur'an (37:99–113) Abraham sees in a dream that he must sacrifice his son, tells him, and the son agrees. As Abraham lays him face down, God calls out that he has fulfilled the vision, and ransoms the son "with a great sacrifice." The son is not named; most Muslims today believe he was Ishmael, and the story is remembered in the hajj and at Eid al-Adha, when animals are sacrificed and the meat shared with the poor.

Kierkegaard (1843) praised Abraham as the "knight of faith" who obeys beyond ethics, and found the story terrifying. Kant (1798) said the opposite: no voice that commands murder can be trusted as God's. Twentieth-century Jewish readers added a third option. Lippman Bodoff argued that God hoped Abraham would refuse, and Omri Boehm that in an earlier form of the story, before the angel's words in 22:11–12 were added, Abraham chose by himself to offer the ram. Critical scholars note that the chapter uses "God" until the angel of "the LORD" stops the knife (22:11), and that Isaac does not come down the mountain (22:19). Most Jewish, Christian and Muslim readers still take the story as Abraham's greatest act of trust.

The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, completed about AD 691, stands over a large outcrop of bedrock. Jewish tradition identifies this rock, the Foundation Stone (Even ha-Shetiyah), with the site of the Holy of Holies and with Mount Moriah. Muslim tradition associates the rock chiefly with Muhammad's Night Journey. The site has not been excavated, so its link with the binding of Isaac rests on tradition, not archaeology.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the test that echoes Hagar's
deep.body: My own reading, close to what several commentators have noticed: Genesis 21 and 22 form a pair. In each, Abraham rises early (21:14; 22:3), gives up a son, and in each the son is about to die in a wild place until an angel calls "from the sky" (21:17; 22:11) and a parent's eyes are opened to see what God provides (a well, 21:19; a ram, 22:13). I suspect the narrator wants us to see that Abraham had already lost one son by obeying God, and that the second test asks whether he will trust God with the son of the promise too. If so, Hagar's story is not a detour but the first half of the test.

echoes: Hebrews 11:17–19; James 2:21–23; Romans 8:32; John 1:29; John 3:16; Mark 1:11; 2 Chronicles 3:1; Hebrews 6:13–18; Acts 3:25; Jeremiah 7:31; Micah 6:7

settings.to: Abraham, living at Beersheba with his son Isaac
settings.when: Some time after the events of chapter 21
settings.why: To test Abraham: take your son, your only one, whom you love, Isaac, and offer him as a burnt offering in the land of Moriah. The command seems to cancel every promise. The readers are told it is a test (22:1); Abraham is not.
settings.readers: For Israel, whose law and prophets condemned child sacrifice (Leviticus 18:21; Jeremiah 7:31), this was a story in which God stops it. 2 Chronicles 3:1 places Mount Moriah where the Temple stood, so Jews linked the Temple's offerings with this mountain.
views: Faith that God can raise the dead
Hebrews 11:17–19 says Abraham reasoned that God could raise Isaac from the dead.
Kierkegaard read the story as faith that goes beyond ethics. Kant said Abraham should have doubted that the voice was God's.
Many scholars read it as a story that replaces the son with a ram. Levenson traces how the idea of the beloved son given up runs through Judaism and Christianity.

settings.to: Each other, on the last climb up the mountain
settings.when: On the third day, as the two walk on together with the wood, the fire and the knife
settings.why: Isaac asks where the lamb for the burnt offering is. Abraham answers, "God will see to the lamb for a burnt offering himself, my son." His words hide the truth from the boy and also hold out a hope he cannot see. They are the only words between father and son in the chapter. The place is later named for them, "The LORD Will See" (22:14).
settings.readers: For Israel the answer became a saying about the Temple mount: "On the mountain of the LORD it will be seen" (22:14). Christians read the lamb God provides as pointing to Christ (John 1:29).
views: Many readers hear in Abraham's answer real trust that God will provide.
Others hear a father who cannot bring himself to tell his son; the rabbis also read it as "God will see to the lamb: you, my son."

settings.by: The angel of the LORD, speaking for the LORD
settings.to: Abraham, on the mountain, after he has offered the ram
settings.when: Right after the binding
settings.why: To swear by God's own self that Abraham will have offspring as many as the stars and the sand. They will take the gate of their enemies. All the nations will bless themselves by his offspring, "because you have listened to my voice." It is the only time in Genesis that God is heard swearing by himself.
settings.readers: For Israel the promise was grounded in its father's obedience. Jews still ask God at the New Year to remember the binding of Isaac.

title: A Grave in the Promised Land
sum: Sarah dies at Hebron at the age of 127, and Abraham mourns her. Then he rises and goes to the town's leaders, the sons of Heth, with a request: "I am a foreigner living among you as a settler. Sell me a piece of ground among you to own as a grave." The townsmen honor him as "a prince of God" and offer him any tomb he likes, but Abraham wants to own one.

In a polite and careful negotiation at the city gate, Abraham asks for the cave of Machpelah belonging to Ephron. Ephron offers to give him the field and cave for nothing, then mentions that it is worth four hundred shekels of silver. Abraham weighs out the full price before witnesses. The field, the cave and its trees pass legally to him, and he buries Sarah there. The first piece of the promised land Abraham owns is a grave.
readings: Read as a legal record
The chapter reads like a contract: the parties, the property, its boundaries, the price, the witnesses. It is written to establish beyond doubt that the tomb at Hebron belonged to Abraham's family.
Read as faith in the promise
Abraham could have buried Sarah in a borrowed tomb. Instead he buys land in Canaan, a sign that he expected his descendants to inherit it (Hebrews 11:13–16).
Read as a portrait of Abraham
In grief, Abraham remains dignified and courteous, bowing to the people of the land. He bargains well and pays without complaint. The man of faith also lives wisely among his neighbors.

views.L: A historical purchase about 2029 BC on the traditional chronology. The cave at Hebron venerated today is the real tomb.
views.F: The chapter's slow pace and repeated words ("hear me," "bury your dead," "in the hearing of") create the feel of a public ceremony. Its theme is the gap between promise and possession: a prince of God who owns nothing.
views.C: Usually assigned to P, which cares about the family tomb (25:9; 49:29–32; 50:13). Some critical scholars date the legal style to the 600s–500s BC and see the story as giving exiled Judeans a claim to Hebron, which was then held by Edomites.
views.J: The Talmud counts Sarah among the seven prophetesses (Megillah 14a), and the Midrash says the cloud of glory rested on her tent, her lamp burned from Sabbath to Sabbath, and her dough was blessed; when Isaac brought Rebekah into the tent, all returned (Genesis Rabbah 60:16; Rashi on 24:67). The Midrash says Machpelah is one of three places Israel bought with full payment, so that the nations could not claim them: the cave, Joseph's tomb at Shechem and the temple site (Genesis Rabbah 79:7).

deep.b: The Herodian enclosure at Hebron is a rectangle of huge cut stones, roughly 195 by 110 feet, with walls rising about 50 to 65 feet, built in the same style as the Western Wall in Jerusalem. Inside are cenotaphs (memorial tombs) for Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob and Leah. The cave below has been seen only a few times; a narrow shaft gives the only regular view.

echoes: Acts 7:5; Acts 7:16; Hebrews 11:9–16; Leviticus 25:23; 1 Chronicles 29:15; 1 Chronicles 21:22–25; Jeremiah 32:6–15; 49:29–32; 50:13

settings.what: The purchase of the cave of Machpelah
settings.by: Abraham, with the sons of Heth and Ephron the Hittite
settings.to: The sons of Heth, the people of the land, gathered at the gate of Hebron, and Ephron
settings.when: After Sarah's death at Hebron
settings.why: To buy a grave rather than receive one as a favor, so that it is his own before witnesses. The polite bargaining hides hard dealing. Ephron "gives" the field and then names a high price, and Abraham pays it in full.
settings.readers: For Israel the speeches were a legal record that the first piece of the promised land was bought, not taken. The ancestors lie in their own ground at Hebron. Judeans who saw Jeremiah buy a field as a sign during the siege (Jeremiah 32) would have understood.
views: Manfred Lehmann compared Hittite laws on the duties tied to owning a whole field.
Gene Tucker and others found closer parallels in later Babylonian sale documents. Some take this as a sign of a later date and others as general ancient custom.

title: A Bride from the East
sum: Abraham, now old, makes his senior servant swear to find a wife for Isaac among his own relatives in Mesopotamia, not among the Canaanites, and never to take Isaac back there. The servant travels with ten camels to the town of Nahor. At the well at evening he prays for a sign: the right young woman will offer water to him and to his camels. Before he finishes, Rebekah appears, granddaughter of Abraham's brother, and does exactly that, drawing water for ten thirsty camels.

The servant gives her gold, worships, and is welcomed into her family's house by her brother Laban. Before eating he tells the whole story again, and the family agrees: "This has come from the LORD." Asked whether she will go, Rebekah says, "I will go." She travels back to Canaan, and at evening Isaac, walking in the field, sees the camels coming. She veils herself. Isaac brings her into his mother's tent, marries her and loves her, and is comforted after Sarah's death.
readings: Read as providence

No miracle happens and no voice speaks, yet the whole chapter is about God guiding ordinary events: "the LORD has led me on the road" (24:27). It is often compared with Ruth and Esther, where God works behind the scenes.
Read as a portrait of faithful service
The servant prays before he acts, worships after each answer, refuses food until his task is done and will not delay his return. He is the model of a trustworthy steward (Luke 12:42).
Read as Rebekah's call
Rebekah's "I will go" repeats Abraham's journey: she leaves land and family to join the covenant family. She is the active figure in the chapter, as she will be in the stories of Jacob and Esau.

views.L: A real journey, about 2026 BC on the traditional count, recorded in detail by the family. The servant is Eliezer, and Rebekah was the historical mother of Jacob and Esau.
views.F: The longest chapter in Genesis is a carefully built story of guidance, in which repetition (the servant's retelling) shows that God's answer matched the prayer exactly. It closes the story of Abraham: the promise passes to Isaac and a new mother enters Sarah's tent.
views.C: Usually assigned to J, though many now see it as a late, independent novella of the Persian period (500s–400s BC), because of its style, its interest in marriage within the family (compare Ezra–Nehemiah) and its view of quiet providence. Others defend an older date.
views.J: The rabbis prized the servant's prayer and drew from 24:57 the rule that a woman's consent is needed for marriage. Rashi says Rebekah was a "rose among thorns," a righteous girl from a family of deceivers. Isaac's meditation in the field is the origin of the afternoon prayer (Berakhot 26b).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the servant as Abraham's last act of faith
deep.body: My own reading: Abraham's last words in Genesis are his instructions to the servant (24:2–8), and they repeat in small the whole of his life. He refuses to let Isaac go back to the old country (as he himself left it, 12:1), he trusts that "the LORD, God of the heavens... will send his angel ahead of you," and he quotes God's promise of the land. The servant's journey is the reverse of Abraham's: from Canaan back to Mesopotamia and home again, bringing someone new into the promise. Abraham never sees the result; the chapter ends with Isaac and Rebekah, not with him. It is a quiet picture of what Hebrews says of all the ancestors: they died "without receiving what was promised; they only saw it and greeted it from far away" (Hebrews 11:13).

echoes: 29:1–20; Exodus 2:15–21; John 4:5–42; Ruth 2:3; Psalm 91:11; Exodus 23:20; Deuteronomy 7:3–4

settings.to: His senior servant, in charge of all he owns
settings.when: When Abraham is old
settings.why: To bind the servant by oath to find Isaac a wife from Abraham's own kin in Mesopotamia, not from the Canaanites. The servant must never take Isaac back there. Both limits guard the promise: the family must stay distinct, and the heir must stay in the land.
settings.readers: For Israel after the exile, marriage with neighboring peoples was a burning question (Ezra 9–10). The charge also spoke to those tempted to stay in Babylon rather than come home.

settings.what: The servant's prayer at the well
settings.to: The LORD, God of his master Abraham
settings.when: At evening, by the well outside the town of Nahor
settings.why: To ask for a sign. The young woman who offers water to him and also to his camels will be the one God has chosen. The test looks for kindness and willingness to work hard. Rebekah answers it before he has finished.
settings.readers: For Israel this was the first prayer for guidance in the Bible, prayed by a nameless servant. It taught that God guides the ordinary steps of a family's life.

settings.to: The LORD, in the hearing of Rebekah
settings.when: When Rebekah tells him she is of Nahor's family
settings.why: To bow and bless the LORD, who has not stopped showing his loyal love and faithfulness to Abraham and has led the servant to the right house. Thanks follows at once on the answered prayer.
settings.readers: For Israel the words "loyal love and faithfulness" were the very words of God's name (Exodus 34:6). The servant's blessing taught Israel to see God's covenant love in a successful journey.

settings.what: The servant's account to Rebekah's family
settings.to: Laban, Bethuel and their household in Aram-naharaim
settings.when: On the evening he arrives, before he will eat
settings.why: To retell the journey and the answered prayer so that the family will agree to the marriage. He shapes the story for them, stressing Abraham's wealth and the LORD's guidance. They answer, "This has come from the LORD."
settings.readers: For Israel the retelling showed God's hand in ordinary events. Even foreigners in Haran could see it.

settings.to: Rebekah, as she leaves to marry Isaac
settings.when: As she sets out with the servant
settings.why: To wish her thousands upon thousands of descendants who will take the gate of their enemies. The words echo the oath to Abraham (22:17), so the hopes of the two branches of the family meet in her.
settings.readers: For Israel, descended from her, it was a blessing on its own mothers. Jewish brides are still blessed with this verse when they are veiled before the wedding.

title: The Death of Abraham and the Birth of Twins
sum: Abraham takes another wife, Keturah, whose sons become tribes of Arabia. He gives everything he has to Isaac and sends the other sons east with gifts. He dies at 175, "old and satisfied," and Isaac and Ishmael bury him beside Sarah in the cave of Machpelah. God blesses Isaac. Ishmael's twelve sons become twelve tribal chiefs, as God promised (17:20), and Ishmael dies at 137.

The account of Isaac begins. Rebekah is barren; Isaac prays and she conceives twins who fight in her womb. The LORD tells her that two nations are inside her and that the elder will serve the younger. Esau is born red and hairy; Jacob follows gripping his heel. Esau grows into a hunter, Isaac's favorite; Jacob stays among the tents, Rebekah's favorite. One day Esau comes in starving and sells his birthright to Jacob for a bowl of red lentil stew.
readings: Read as a passing of generations
The chapter ties off Abraham's story with his death and the lines of his other sons, then opens the story of Isaac. Genesis moves on through the "family history" (toledot) of each heir (25:12, 19).
Read as God's choice
Before the twins are born, God announces that the younger will rule. The rest of Jacob's story shows that choice working out through human weakness (Romans 9:10–13).
Read as a story of nations
Ishmael's tribes, Keturah's tribes and Esau's Edom are all Israel's neighbors. Genesis tells their origins as family stories, showing kinship as well as rivalry.

views.L: Abraham dies about 1991 BC on the traditional chronology (Ussher's dates are about 170 years later). The genealogies record real persons whose families became tribes, and the oracle to Rebekah is a true prophecy fulfilled in Israel and Edom.
views.F: The chapter is a hinge. Two toledot headings (25:12, 19) close Abraham's age and open Isaac's. The birth story and the stew scene work as a prologue to the whole Jacob cycle: rivalry, favoritism, the younger son overtaking the elder, and wordplays on red, hair and heel.
views.C: The death notice, ages and lists are usually assigned to P (25:7–11a, 12–17, 19–20, 26b), and the birth and stew stories to J. The tribal names fit Arabian peoples best known in the 800s–500s BC. Many scholars read Esau and Jacob as figures of Edom and Israel, with the stories explaining Israel's rule over Edom under David.
views.J: The Midrash says Abraham died five years early so that he would not see Esau go astray, and that Jacob's lentils were the mourners' meal (Genesis Rabbah 63:12; Bava Batra 16b). Esau and Edom became the rabbis' name for Rome. The Torah portion Toledot begins at 25:19.

deep.title: Ishmael's tribes in the record
deep.b: Assyrian kings of the 700s–600s BC fought "Arabs" called Qedar (Kedar) and Nabayati (Nebaioth), and an Arab queen of Qedar paid tribute to Sennacherib. Dumah (Dumat al-Jandal) and Tema (Tayma) were caravan oases on the routes north from Arabia, and inscriptions at Tayma record the Babylonian king Nabonidus's long stay there. Whether the Nabayati are the later Nabataeans of Petra is debated: the spelling of the two names differs.

Genesis keeps passing over the firstborn: Abel over Cain, Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Joseph and Judah over Reuben, Ephraim over Manasseh. In the ancient world the eldest son was expected to inherit, so the pattern stands out. One reading is that God's choice rests on grace, not birth order (Romans 9:11). Another, common among critical scholars, is that Genesis is quietly explaining how Israel, a latecomer among the peoples of its region, could be the chosen line. The two readings do not exclude each other.

settings.to: Rebekah, troubled by the twins struggling inside her
settings.when: When she goes to ask the LORD
settings.why: To tell her that two nations are in her womb, that one will be stronger, and that "the elder will serve the younger." The oracle frames the whole Jacob story.
settings.readers: For Israel the twins were Israel and Edom. David's conquest of Edom (2 Samuel 8:14) and Edom's later revolt (2 Kings 8:20–22) were read in its light. Paul uses it to show that God's choice does not rest on what people do (Romans 9:10–13).

settings.to: Each other, at Jacob's stew pot
settings.when: When Esau comes in from the wild, worn out
settings.why: Jacob makes Esau swear away his birthright, the firstborn's larger share and leadership, for a meal of stew. The short exchange shows Esau despising his birthright and Jacob grasping for it. It also explains the name Edom, "red."
settings.readers: For Israel this was a chance to laugh at the ancestor of a rival nation, while also seeing its own father's craftiness. Hebrews 12:16 holds Esau up as a warning.
